newsitem.title: USA: Corn, soybean prices drop to 10-month lows.
newsitem.headline: Corn, soybean prices drop to 10-month lows.

text.p: Surprising increases in government crop estimates launched a wave of selling in commodity markets Friday that sent corn prices to their lowest level in 10 months and soybeans to a nine-month low.
Cotton and orange juice prices also tumbled after the Agriculture Department's crop report.
The declines were reflected in the Commodity Research Bureau's index of 17 commodities that fell 1.68 points to 245.70.
Soybeans tumbled the 30-cent daily limit, soymeal fell the $10 limit and soyoil also fell sharply.

The department raised its estimates for this year's corn crop to 9.01 billion bushels, which would be the third largest on record, from its previous estimate of 8.80 billion bushels. It raised its soybean estimate to 2.35 billion bushels, which would be the second largest ever, from 2.27 billion.
"There's nothing friendly about the corn or bean numbers," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities.

Corn for December delivery fell 6-1/4 cents to $2.83-3/4 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade, the lowest since December 1995. November soybeans fell the daily 30-cent limit to $7.00-1/4 a bushel, the lowest since January.

CBOT December soymeal closed down the $10 limit at $233.50 a ton, and December soyoil was down 0.99 at 22.61 cents a pound. Soymeal is a key livestock feed ingredient and soyoil is widely used in processed food, paints and inks.
The selling spilled into Canada, where prices for canola, an oilseed that competes with soybeans, fell the maximum $10 a metric ton limit at the Winnipeg Commodity Exchange.
In its first estimate of the year, the department also pegged the domestic orange crop at 220 million 20-pound boxes, well above industry estimates and last year's crop of 203.2 million boxes.

That news, coupled with reports of slowing demand, fuelled selling of frozen concentrated orange juice futures. The November contract fell 0.95 cent to 111.25 cents a pound at the New York Cotton Exchange.
Cotton futures also fell, erasing gains from a month-long rally. Traders were shocked when the government raised its U.S. crop estimate and slashed usage.
"This report is not neutral but decisively bearish," said Sharon Johnson, an analyst with Frank Schneider and Co. Inc.

The department estimated the cotton crop at 18.19 million 480-pound bales, vs. its September estimate of 17.90 million. Ending stocks, which remain after mill and export needs are met, were increased to 4.5 million bales from 3.6 million.
December cotton fell 2.20 cents to 73.20 cents a pound at the New York Cotton Exchange.
Gasoline prices jumped at the New York Mercantile Exchange on momentum from news early this week showing drops in production and imports.
Gasoline for November delivery rose 2 cents to 65.52 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange, nearly offsetting Thursday's 2.07-cent loss.
Crude oil for November delivery rose 40 cents to $24.66 a barrel and November heating oil was up 0.51 cent to 71.43 cents a gallon.
